law: Knowledge Once — commerce substance defined here once, projected everywhere. Commerce objects are PROJECTIONS, never stored as truth.

COM.concepts: Universal Commerce projects commercial reality from primitives. A commercial object = Existence + Knowledge + Meaning + Relationships + Context + Policies + Authorities + Time. Products, services, bundles, offers, subscriptions, contracts, licenses, memberships, listings, assets, and experiences are all projections — never stored, never hardcoded.
COM.ontology: Commerce is a Reality type (Commercial Reality), not a domain of stored objects. Commercial projection is a pure function of primitives resolved within a Context.
COM.taxonomy: By projection: Product / Service / Bundle / Offer / Subscription / Contract / License / Membership / Listing / Asset / Experience. By model: One-time / Recurring / Usage / Consignment / Marketplace / Hybrid. By channel: Any (channel is a Context, not a type).
COM.dataModel:
```yaml
CommercialProjection:
  projectionId: <Identity>
  existence: <Identity>
  knowledge: [<Knowledge>]
  meaning: <SemanticModel>
  relationships: [<Relationship>]
  context: <Context>
  policies: [<Policy>]
  authorities: [<Authority>]
  temporal: {asOf, validIn}
  projectionHash: <content-addressed>
```
COM.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Composing
    Composing --> Projected
    Projected --> Published
    Published --> Withdrawn
    Published --> Stale: primitives changed
    Stale --> Composing
```
workflow: resolve existence → gather knowledge + meaning → traverse relationships → apply context + policies → project → publish with hash
authorities: Context Authority (what may be projected in scope); Merchant Authority (publication).
COM.privacy: Projections involving personal data minimize via Perspective before publication; commercial identity is pseudonymous by default.
COM.audit: Every projection records its primitive inputs and hash, so any commercial object is reproducible and its history reconstructable.
COM.twin: Commercial Twin mirrors the real-world commercial state (availability, status, ownership) continuously from observations.
COM.agent: Commerce Agent detects projection staleness when primitives change and re-projects under governance.
COM.runtime: Projections are computed and content-hashed; caching keyed by input primitive versions guarantees consistency.
COM.scaling: Projection is parallelizable per existence; catalog reads serve cached hashes with primitive-version invalidation.
COM.multiTenant: Commerce projections are strictly tenant-scoped; cross-tenant catalog requires published marketplace relationship.
COM.geo: Contextual distribution is projection-time: language, currency, tax, compliance are applied from the Context registry — never compiled in.
COM.failure: Primitive staleness, context policy conflict, authority gap, hash mismatch on re-projection.
COM.recovery: Projections are pure functions of primitives — recovery is re-derivation, never restore.
COM.certification: Projection must pass primitive-conformance (zero hardcoded commerce terms), context validity, and hash reproducibility.
COM.migration: New commercial models are registry additions to projection types; no schema migration ever touches primitives.
COM.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant CO as Commerce Engine
    participant CT as Context
    C->>CO: project(existence)
    CO->>CT: resolve commercial context
    CT-->>CO: context + policies
    CO->>CO: compose projection
    CO-->>C: CommerceProjected (hashed)
```
COM.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Resolving
    Resolving --> Composing
    Composing --> Hashing
    Hashing --> Published
```
COM.blueprint: Build order for COM: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by projection: product / service / bundle / offer / subscription / contract / license / membership / listing / asset / experience as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (commerce.project, commerce.reproject, commerce.publish) and validate against COM boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

GPS.concepts: Global Products & Services supports all industries, categories, product types, service types, business models, languages, currencies, regions, countries, territories, marketplaces, channels, and future commercial domains without redesign. This is achieved because none of those concepts exist in the platform — they are registry entries projected at runtime.
GPS.ontology: A product or service is an Existence with commercial projections. Industry, category, brand, and channel are Context and Semantic constructs, not schema fields.
GPS.taxonomy: By projection type: Product / Service / Digital / Physical / Hybrid / Future. By model: any registry-defined commercial model. By reach: Local / National / Global / Future.
GPS.dataModel:
```yaml
GlobalCatalogEntry:
  existence: <Identity>
  semanticConcept: <SemanticModel>   # 'phone' across all languages
  classifications: [<Taxonomy node>]
  contexts: [<Context>]               # where it is offered
  commercialProjections: [<CommercialProjection>]
  localization: [{locale, projection}]
```
GPS.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Resolved
    Resolved --> Listed
    Listed --> Featured
    Listed --> Delisted
    Delisted --> [*]
```
workflow: resolve existence + semantic concept → classify per context → localize per locale → list under context policy
GPS.privacy: Catalog entries with personal attribution (e.g., artisan provenance) require consent scope.
GPS.audit: Every listing and localization records authority, context, and semantic version.
GPS.twin: Catalog Twin tracks real-world availability and lifecycle state across all contexts.
GPS.agent: Catalog Agent auto-completes semantics, detects duplicates across locales, and proposes classifications.
GPS.runtime: Resolution is locale-aware with semantic disambiguation; catalog reads are the hottest path and heavily cached.
GPS.scaling: Globally replicated read layer; write path is authority-gated and low-throughput.
GPS.multiTenant: Catalogs are tenant-scoped; a shared marketplace aggregates with explicit published relationship.
GPS.geo: Localization and compliance projection are per-region; the same existence projects differently per jurisdiction.
GPS.failure: Semantic ambiguity across locales, category orphaning, context policy conflict, stale localization.
GPS.recovery: Entries re-project from primitives; localization history is versioned and reversible.
GPS.certification: Entry must pass semantic uniqueness, classification validity, and localization completeness.
GPS.migration: New locales/industries are registry additions — zero downtime, zero schema change.
GPS.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant GC as Catalog
    participant SE as Semantic
    C->>GC: resolve(surface, locale)
    GC->>SE: disambiguate concept
    SE-->>GC: concept
    GC->>GC: classify + localize
    GC-->>C: localized entry
```
GPS.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Disambiguating
    Disambiguating --> Classifying
    Classifying --> Localizing
    Localizing --> Listed
```
GPS.blueprint: Build order for GPS: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by projection type: product / service / digital / physical / hybrid / future as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (catalog.resolve, catalog.localize, catalog.feature) and validate against GPS boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

PRC.concepts: Pricing is a projection of value under context — never a stored attribute. Price depends on cost knowledge, market context, customer context, competitive relationships, time, and policy. The same existence has infinitely many valid prices across contexts.
PRC.ontology: Price is a function: f(cost, market, customer, competitor, time, policy) → monetary expression. Currency is a Context property; tax is a Policy projection.
PRC.taxonomy: By model: Static / Dynamic / Usage / Tiered / Negotiated / Auction / Future model (registry). By dimension: List / Spot / Contract / Promotional.
PRC.dataModel:
```yaml
PricingProjection:
  existence: <Identity>
  baseExpression: <registry expression>
  modifiers: [<registry modifier>]
  currencyUnit: <Context-derived>
  taxProjection: <Policy-derived>
  context: <Context>
  temporal: {asOf}
  confidence: <0..1>
```
PRC.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Quoting
    Quoting --> Quoted
    Quoted --> Frozen: committed to contract
    Quoted --> Stale: context changed
    Stale --> Quoting
    Frozen --> [*]
```
workflow: resolve cost knowledge → apply market context → apply customer context → apply policy modifiers → project currency + tax → quote
authorities: Pricing Authority (model governance); merchant authority sets base within policy bounds.
PRC.privacy: Customer-specific pricing is personal data; quotes are consent-scoped and retention-limited.
PRC.audit: Every quote records the full input set — cost, context, policy version — so it is reproducible and explainable.
PRC.twin: Pricing Twin mirrors real-world price observations (competitor feeds, market data) and flags drift from model output.
PRC.agent: Pricing Agent continuously re-quotes on context change and runs simulations before applying adjustments.
PRC.runtime: Quoting is a deterministic function evaluation cached by input hash; staleness invalidates on context/policy change.
PRC.scaling: Quote caching is the critical path; evaluation is sub-millisecond with precompiled modifier chains.
PRC.multiTenant: Pricing models are tenant-scoped; a shared marketplace sees only published prices, not competitor internals.
PRC.geo: Currency, tax, and duty projection are jurisdiction-derived at quote time — never hardcoded per market.
PRC.failure: Circular modifier dependencies, policy conflict, stale market feed, currency conversion failure.
PRC.recovery: Quotes recompute from inputs; frozen prices are immutable contract artifacts.
PRC.certification: Pricing model must pass determinism, policy conformance, and currency/tax projection validity.
PRC.migration: New pricing models and modifiers are registry additions.
PRC.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant PR as Pricing
    participant PL as Policy
    C->>PR: quote(existence, context)
    PR->>PL: resolve pricing policy
    PL-->>PR: modifiers
    PR->>PR: evaluate model
    PR-->>C: quote
```
PRC.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Costing
    Costing --> Contextualizing
    Contextualizing --> Modifying
    Modifying --> Quoting
```
PRC.blueprint: Build order for PRC: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by model: static / dynamic / usage / tiered / negotiated / auction / future model (registry) as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (pricing.quote, pricing.adjust, pricing.simulate) and validate against PRC boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

OFR.concepts: An Offer is a time-bounded, context-bound commercial projection bundling existence, pricing, and terms under policy. Offers are ephemeral by nature — they are not things, they are proposals.
OFR.ontology: Offer has a subject existence, a pricing projection, terms (policy-derived), a temporal window, and a context. Bundles are offers over multiple existences with relationship rules.
OFR.taxonomy: By structure: Single / Bundle / Configurable / Tiered. By temporality: Flash / Standing / Seasonal / Evergreen. By targeting: Universal / Segment / Individual (consent-gated).
OFR.dataModel:
```yaml
OfferProjection:
  offerId: <Identity>
  subjects: [<Identity>]
  pricingProjection: <PricingProjection>
  terms: [<Policy>]
  context: <Context>
  temporal: {startsAt, endsAt}
  eligibility: <registry expression>
  status: <Draft|Active|Expired|Redeemed>
```
OFR.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft
    Draft --> Active: startsAt reached
    Active --> Redeemed
    Active --> Expired: endsAt reached
    Active --> Extended
    Redeemed --> [*]
    Expired --> [*]
```
workflow: compose subjects + pricing → attach terms → set eligibility → activate → redeem under policy → expire
authorities: Merchant Authority (creation), Pricing Authority (price validity), Policy Authority (terms).
OFR.privacy: Individual-targeted offers require consent; segment targeting is aggregated only.
OFR.audit: Every redemption records offer version, pricing inputs, and policy evaluation — the basis of revenue audit.
OFR.twin: Offer Twin tracks real-world redemption patterns and predicts uptake for simulation.
OFR.agent: Offer Agent proposes and tunes offers from observed demand, under pricing and policy governance.
OFR.runtime: Eligibility is a policy evaluation cached per (offer, subject-segment); redemption is idempotent.
OFR.scaling: Read-heavy during active windows; redemption is transactional and sharded by offer.
OFR.multiTenant: Offers are tenant-scoped; cross-tenant offers require marketplace relationship and both merchants' authority.
OFR.geo: Offer validity is jurisdiction-projected — terms legal in one region may not be offered in another.
OFR.failure: Temporal inversion, eligibility policy conflict, over-redemption, pricing drift mid-offer.
OFR.recovery: Redemptions are immutable events; expired offers are historical artifacts, never deleted.
OFR.certification: Offer must pass temporal validity, policy conformance, pricing version pinning, and eligibility determinism.
OFR.migration: New offer structures are registry additions.
OFR.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Merchant
    participant OF as Offer Domain
    participant PL as Policy
    M->>OF: create(subjects, terms)
    OF->>PL: validate terms
    PL-->>OF: compliant
    OF->>OF: activate at startsAt
    OF-->>M: OfferActivated
```
OFR.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Composing
    Composing --> Validating
    Validating --> Active
    Active --> Redeemed
```
OFR.blueprint: Build order for OFR: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by structure: single / bundle / configurable / tiered as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (offer.create, offer.activate, offer.expire) and validate against OFR boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

SUB.concepts: A Subscription is a temporal, policy-governed recurring relationship — not a stored object. It is the projection of an ongoing commercial relationship with entitlement, obligation, and lifecycle.
SUB.ontology: Subscription has a subject, a subscriber, an entitlement (policy projection), a billing schedule (projection), and a lifecycle state machine. It is a specialized Relationship type projected commercially.
SUB.taxonomy: By cadence: Fixed-period / Usage-based / Milestone / Event-driven. By commitment: Evergreen / Term / Auto-renew / Trial. By entitlement: Tiered / Per-seat / Volume / Custom.
SUB.dataModel:
```yaml
SubscriptionProjection:
  subscriptionId: <Identity>
  relationship: <Relationship>   # the underlying truth
  entitlements: [<Policy>]
  cadence: <registry expression>
  temporal: {startedAt, currentPeriod, renewAt}
  lifecycleState: <registry state>
  context: <Context>
```
SUB.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Trial
    Trial --> Active: converted
    Trial --> Expired
    Active --> Suspended: payment failure
    Suspended --> Active: recovered
    Active --> Upgraded
    Active --> Cancelled
    Cancelled --> ExpiredAtTerm
    ExpiredAtTerm --> [*]
```
workflow: create relationship → attach entitlement policy → schedule cadence → bill → renew/cancel per policy → expire
authorities: Merchant Authority (terms), Holder Authority (cancel/modify), Billing Authority (schedule).
SUB.privacy: Subscription history is personal data; retention follows consent and legal basis (contract performance).
SUB.audit: Every lifecycle transition records the triggering event, policy applied, and authority — full reconstructable history.
SUB.twin: Subscription Twin mirrors real-world service delivery state against entitlement — detecting over- or under-delivery.
SUB.agent: Subscription Agent monitors renewal risk, payment failures, and usage-vs-entitlement gaps, acting within policy.
SUB.runtime: Lifecycle is an event-driven state machine; cadence is a scheduler projection, not a polling loop.
SUB.scaling: Renewal waves are smoothed across periods; billing is sharded by holder.
SUB.multiTenant: Subscriptions never cross tenants; marketplace subscriptions involve both tenants' authority.
SUB.geo: Cancellation and renewal terms are jurisdiction-projected — consumer protection policy applies locally.
SUB.failure: Entitlement drift, cadence slip, orphaned billing, policy conflict on upgrade.
SUB.recovery: State machine is event-sourced; recovery replays transitions. Suspended state auto-recovers per policy.
SUB.certification: Subscription must pass entitlement-policy conformance, cadence validity, and lifecycle determinism.
SUB.migration: New cadences and entitlement models are registry additions.
SUB.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant H as Holder
    participant SU as Subscription Domain
    participant BL as Billing
    H->>SU: create(subject)
    SU->>BL: schedule cadence
    BL-->>SU: scheduled
    SU->>SU: activate
    SU-->>H: SubscriptionCreated
```
SUB.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Entitled
    Entitled --> Scheduled
    Scheduled --> Active
    Active --> Renewed
```
SUB.blueprint: Build order for SUB: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by cadence: fixed-period / usage-based / milestone / event-driven as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (subscription.create, subscription.renew, subscription.cancel) and validate against SUB boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

CNT.concepts: A Contract is a projection — an agreement whose truth lives in relationships, policies, authorities, evidence, and signatures. The platform never stores 'a contract' as a business object; it stores the primitives that make one enforceable and projects the contract at runtime.
CNT.ontology: Contract = Parties (relationships) + Terms (policies) + Signatures (evidence) + Obligations (rules) + Jurisdiction (context). Its enforceability is computed, not assumed.
CNT.taxonomy: By formation: Signed / Implicit / Programmatic / Smart. By duration: One-time / Term / Evergreen. By enforceability: Executed / Executory / Void / Voidable.
CNT.dataModel:
```yaml
ContractProjection:
  contractId: <Identity>
  parties: [<Relationship>]
  terms: [<Policy>]
  obligations: [<Rule>]
  signatures: [<Evidence>]
  jurisdiction: <Context>
  temporal: {executedAt, effectiveFrom, terminatesAt}
  enforceability: <Trust>
```
CNT.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Drafted
    Drafted --> Signed
    Signed --> Executed
    Executed --> Performed
    Executed --> Breached
    Executed --> Disputed
    Disputed --> Terminated
    Performed --> [*]
    Terminated --> [*]
```
workflow: form terms → bind parties → collect signature evidence → compute enforceability → execute → trigger obligations → perform/terminate
authorities: Each party's authority signs; jurisdiction authority governs enforceability computation.
CNT.privacy: Contract contents are access-restricted to parties and jurisdiction authorities; metadata is auditable.
CNT.audit: Every amendment, obligation trigger, and dispute is preserved with evidence. The contract's full lifecycle is reconstructable.
CNT.twin: Contract Twin tracks real-world performance against obligations — delivering, delaying, breaching.
CNT.agent: Contract Agent monitors obligation triggers, detects breach risk, and escalates disputes under governance.
CNT.runtime: Obligation evaluation is rule-driven and event-triggered; enforceability is a trust computation over signatures.
CNT.scaling: Contracts are low-write, high-audit; sharded by jurisdiction for sovereignty.
CNT.multiTenant: Contracts bind tenants via relationships; cross-tenant contracts require both authorities.
CNT.geo: Jurisdiction is a first-class field — the same terms project differently across legal systems.
CNT.failure: Missing signature authority, term conflict, jurisdiction gap, evidence revocation.
CNT.recovery: Amendments append; nothing is overwritten. Voiding is a recorded outcome with full history retained.
CNT.certification: Contract must pass signature completeness, term-policy conformance, and jurisdiction validity to be enforceable.
CNT.migration: New term types and contract kinds are registry additions.
CNT.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Party A
    participant CN as Contract Domain
    participant B as Party B
    A->>CN: draft terms
    CN->>B: request signature
    B->>CN: sign (evidence)
    CN->>CN: compute enforceability
    CN-->>A: ContractExecuted
```
CNT.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Drafting
    Drafting --> Signing
    Signing --> Executing
    Executing --> Performing
```
CNT.blueprint: Build order for CNT: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by formation: signed / implicit / programmatic / smart as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (contract.form, contract.amend, contract.execute) and validate against CNT boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

MKT.concepts: A Marketplace is a Context type — a governed environment where multiple tenants' projections are visible under a shared policy set. It is not a stored object; it is a scope in which commerce projections aggregate.
MKT.ontology: Marketplace has Participants (tenants with published relationships), Listing policies, Discovery mechanisms, and a governing Context. Participation is governed by relationship, not by code.
MKT.taxonomy: By model: First-party / Third-party / Hybrid / Consignment. By governance: Open / Curated / Invite-only. By scope: Local / National / Global.
MKT.dataModel:
```yaml
MarketplaceContext:
  marketplaceId: <Identity>
  context: <Context>
  participants: [<Relationship>]
  listingPolicy: <Policy>
  discoveryPolicy: <Policy>
  governance: <Authority>
  temporal: {effectiveFrom}
```
MKT.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Applicant
    Applicant --> Participant: approved
    Participant --> Suspended
    Suspended --> Participant
    Participant --> Left
    Left --> [*]
```
workflow: apply under listing policy → approve via governance relationship → list projections → govern discovery → exit
authorities: Marketplace Authority (governance), Merchant Authority (their own listings).
MKT.privacy: Participant identity exposure follows the marketplace's published privacy policy and participant consent.
MKT.audit: Every listing and governance action records authority and policy version.
MKT.twin: Marketplace Twin aggregates participant twins into fleet-level health and emergence monitoring.
MKT.agent: Marketplace Agent curates quality, detects policy violations, and proposes discovery optimizations.
MKT.runtime: Discovery is a context-filtered search over aggregated projections; ranking is policy-driven.
MKT.scaling: Search is the scaling bottleneck — handled by the Search Architecture with context-aware sharding.
MKT.multiTenant: Marketplace is inherently multi-tenant — the only place projections aggregate, under explicit policy.
MKT.geo: A marketplace spanning jurisdictions partitions by jurisdiction policy; illegal cross-listings are projected out.
MKT.failure: Policy conflict between marketplace and participant, discovery bias, listing spam, governance deadlock.
MKT.recovery: Participation is relationship-driven; leaving is clean and reversible by re-application.
MKT.certification: Marketplace must publish its listing and discovery policies and prove their enforcement.
MKT.migration: New marketplace models are registry additions.
MKT.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Merchant
    participant MK as Marketplace
    participant PL as Policy
    M->>MK: apply
    MK->>PL: evaluate listing policy
    PL-->>MK: approved
    MK->>MK: index projections
    MK-->>M: MarketplaceJoined
```
MKT.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Applying
    Applying --> Vetting
    Vetting --> Participating
    Participating --> Indexed
```

Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

INV.concepts: Inventory is a projection of availability — the relationship between an existence and a location-context, quantified and time-stamped. It is a continuously-observed approximation, never absolute truth.
INV.ontology: Inventory has a subject existence, a location Context, a quantity, an observation basis, and uncertainty. Multiple inventory projections may disagree across contexts — the contradiction is preserved, not averaged away.
INV.taxonomy: By location: Physical / Digital / Virtual / Transit. By certainty: Observed / Computed / Projected / Unknown. By reservation: Available / Reserved / Committed / Quarantined.
INV.dataModel:
```yaml
InventoryProjection:
  inventoryId: <Identity>
  subject: <Identity>
  location: <Context>
  quantity: <number>
  unit: <registry id>
  observationBasis: <Observation|null>
  uncertainty: <Uncertainty>
  reservationState: <registry state>
  temporal: {asOf}
```
INV.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Observed
    Observed --> Available
    Available --> Reserved
    Reserved --> Committed
    Reserved --> Released
    Available --> Quarantined
    Quarantined --> Available
    Committed --> [*]
```
workflow: observe → apply uncertainty → resolve contradictions per policy → expose availability → reserve under policy → commit on fulfillment
authorities: Location Authority (observation validity), Merchant Authority (reservation policy).
INV.privacy: Inventory over personal holdings is consent-scoped; aggregate availability is public per marketplace policy.
INV.audit: Every observation and reservation records source, time, and uncertainty — stock claims are evidence-backed.
INV.twin: Inventory Twin mirrors real-world stock continuously and predicts stockout risk for simulation.
INV.agent: Inventory Agent detects drift between observed and computed inventory and triggers reconciliation under policy.
INV.runtime: Availability is a read-side projection over the observation stream; reservations are transactional and short-lived.
INV.scaling: Observation stream is high-throughput; availability is cached per (subject, location) with stream invalidation.
INV.multiTenant: Inventories are tenant-scoped; marketplace aggregates only published availability.
INV.geo: Location context implies residency — cross-border availability respects export and sovereignty policy.
INV.failure: Contradiction deadlock, observation starvation, over-reservation, unit mismatch.
INV.recovery: Availability recomputes from the observation stream; reservations expire safely by policy.
INV.certification: Inventory claim must carry observation basis and uncertainty — unsourced quantities are non-certifiable.
INV.migration: New units and location types are registry additions.
INV.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Source
    participant IN as Inventory Domain
    participant OB as Observation
    S->>IN: observe(quantity, location)
    IN->>OB: record observation
    OB-->>IN: acknowledged
    IN->>IN: reconcile + expose
    IN-->>S: InventoryObserved
```
INV.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Observing
    Observing --> Reconciling
    Reconciling --> Exposing
    Exposing --> Reservable
```

ORD.concepts: An Order is a projection of intent — a sequence of decisions committing parties to exchanges. Its truth lives in the underlying relationships, policies, decisions, and evidence, not in a stored order object.
ORD.ontology: Order = Intent + Parties (relationships) + Terms (policy) + Decisions (lifecycle) + Evidence (fulfillment). State transitions are governed decisions, not mutations.
ORD.taxonomy: By fulfillment: Immediate / Scheduled / Pre-order / Backorder / Digital-instant. By origin: Direct / Marketplace / Subscription / Agent-initiated. By state: Pre-purchase / Committed / In-progress / Complete / Disrupted.
ORD.dataModel:
```yaml
OrderProjection:
  orderId: <Identity>
  intent: <Intent>
  parties: [<Relationship>]
  lines: [{existence, quantity, pricingProjection}]
  decisions: [<Decision>]
  evidence: [<Evidence>]
  lifecycleState: <registry state>
  context: <Context>
  temporal: {placedAt}
```
ORD.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Cart
    Cart --> Placed
    Placed --> Confirmed: payment evidence
    Confirmed --> InProgress
    InProgress --> Shipped
    Shipped --> Delivered
    Delivered --> Completed
    Placed --> Cancelled
    Confirmed --> Disputed
    Disputed --> Resolved
    Completed --> [*]
```
workflow: capture intent → validate under policy → confirm with payment evidence → progress via governed decisions → complete with fulfillment evidence
authorities: Buyer Authority (place/cancel), Merchant Authority (fulfill), Platform Authority (dispute resolution).
ORD.privacy: Orders are rich personal data — access strictly party-scoped, retention per legal basis and consent.
ORD.audit: Every transition is a recorded decision with authority, policy, and evidence. The order's full history is an audit artifact.
ORD.twin: Order Twin mirrors real-world fulfillment and flags disruption between committed and observed state.
ORD.agent: Order Agent monitors progression, predicts disruption, and initiates recovery actions within policy.
ORD.runtime: Lifecycle is an event-sourced state machine; transitions are policy-guarded and idempotent.
ORD.scaling: Placed orders are transactional and sharded by buyer; reads are served from the event projection.
ORD.multiTenant: Orders bind tenants via relationships; marketplace orders carry both authorities.
ORD.geo: Order terms project per jurisdiction — tax, duty, and consumer rights applied locally.
ORD.failure: Evidence gap at confirmation, transition policy conflict, split-brain on reroute, dispute deadlock.
ORD.recovery: Event sourcing replays to any state; cancellations are compensating events, not deletes.
ORD.certification: Every transition must be policy-authorized and evidence-backed — silent mutations void certification.
ORD.migration: New lifecycle states are registry additions; existing orders keep their state-machine version.
ORD.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Buyer
    participant OR as Order Domain
    participant EV as Evidence
    B->>OR: place(intent, lines)
    OR->>OR: validate under policy
    OR->>EV: bind payment evidence
    EV-->>OR: confirmed
    OR-->>B: OrderPlaced
```
ORD.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Intending
    Intending --> Validating
    Validating --> Evidencing
    Evidencing --> Committed
```
ORD.blueprint: Build order for ORD: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by fulfillment: immediate / scheduled / pre-order / backorder / digital-instant as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (order.place, order.transition, order.cancel) and validate against ORD boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

FUL.concepts: Fulfillment is the projection of commitment becoming reality — moving an order's promise to an observed outcome. It is the bridge between commercial projection and physical/digital reality, driven by evidence at every step.
FUL.ontology: Fulfillment has an Order projection, a plan (workflow projection), checkpoints (decisions + evidence), and an outcome. Disruption is a first-class state, not an error.
FUL.taxonomy: By mode: Ship / Pickup / Digital-delivery / Service-render / Return / Exchange. By stage: Planned / In-motion / Delivered / Verified / Disrupted / Recovered. By control: First-party / Third-party / Dropship / Hybrid.
FUL.dataModel:
```yaml
FulfillmentProjection:
  fulfillmentId: <Identity>
  orderRef: <OrderProjection>
  plan: <workflow projection>
  checkpoints: [{decision, evidence, temporal}]
  outcome: <registry state>
  context: <Context>
  disruption: <Contradiction|null>
```
FUL.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planned
    Planned --> InMotion
    InMotion --> Checkpointed
    Checkpointed --> InMotion
    Checkpointed --> Delivered
    Delivered --> Verified: evidence matches
    Delivered --> Disrupted: evidence contradicts
    Disrupted --> Recovered
    Verified --> Completed
    Completed --> [*]
```
workflow: plan workflow under policy → execute → record checkpoint decisions + evidence → verify delivery against promise → complete or disrupt+recover
authorities: Fulfiller Authority (execution), Merchant Authority (plan), Buyer Authority (acceptance evidence).
FUL.privacy: Fulfillment data is personal; tracking exposure follows consent and minimization — location granularity policy-governed.
FUL.audit: Every checkpoint records what happened, why, who authorized, which policy allowed, and what evidence supports it.
FUL.twin: Fulfillment Twin tracks the real-world movement and is the primary source of disruption detection.
FUL.agent: Fulfillment Agent detects disruption early, proposes recovery (reroute, expedite, substitute), and acts within policy bounds.
FUL.runtime: Checkpoint ingestion is a high-throughput stream; state is an event-sourced machine with idempotent checkpoints.
FUL.scaling: Sharded by fulfiller; tracking reads are cached with stream invalidation.
FUL.multiTenant: Third-party fulfillment is a governed relationship — data shared only within policy scope.
FUL.geo: Cross-border fulfillment respects export controls, customs, and sovereignty policy at planning time.
FUL.failure: Evidence contradiction, checkpoint starvation, plan policy conflict, recovery loop.
FUL.recovery: Disruption is a state with a governed recovery workflow — not an exception path. Every recovery is audited.
FUL.certification: Delivery claims require matching evidence; unverifiable deliveries are Disrupted, not Completed.
FUL.migration: New fulfillment modes are registry additions.
FUL.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fulfiller
    participant FU as Fulfillment Domain
    participant TW as Twin
    F->>FU: checkpoint(evidence)
    FU->>TW: compare to twin state
    TW-->>FU: match/contradiction
    alt match
        FU-->>F: CheckpointRecorded
    else contradiction
        FU-->>F: FulfillmentDisrupted
    end
```
FUL.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planning
    Planning --> Executing
    Executing --> Evidencing
    Evidencing --> Verifying
    Verifying --> Completed
```
